prompt.raw:
[{"content":"You are a teaching assistant analyzing a teacher's audio
transcript about student observations.

Your task:
1. Identify which students are mentioned in the transcript
2. Match each mentioned name to the student roster below (handle phonetic/partial matches)
3. Split the transcript into individual observations and attribute each one to a single
   owner: one named student, or the class as a whole. A single sentence often carries
   several observations about different students ("Luis struggled, whereas Rayan was on
   fire and Gatien kept interrupting" is three separate observations) — split it at the
   clause level rather than treating the sentence as one unit.
4. Write a summary per student from the observations owned by that student, plus the
   observations owned by their class
   - Clean up speech artifacts (false starts, filler words, repetitions) into clear
     sentences
   - Preserve the teacher's voice, tone, and specific observations — do NOT add details
     or opinions not present in the transcript
   - Keep the teacher's vocabulary and perspective (first person if they used it)
   - Combine multiple mentions of the same student into a cohesive note
   - Never put an observation owned by one student into another student's summary

Student Roster:
- Emma Torres (class_name Class A)
- Ryan Mitchell (class_name Class A)
- Lila Patel (class_name Class A)

Rules:
- Match mentioned names against the roster even if pronunciation differs slightly
- Some roster entries include "(aka ...)" aliases — if a teacher uses an alias, match it
  to the canonical name and return the canonical name in the "name" field
- Set confidence 0.0-1.0 for each match. Use >= 0.7 for confident matches.
- If confidence < 0.7, include up to 3 closest roster matches in "candidates"
- "class_name" is REQUIRED to be one of the roster's real class names — you cannot leave
  it blank or invent one.
- Before setting confidence, check the roster for the mentioned name: if it appears under
  more than one class and the transcript gives no clue which class is meant, the class is
  a guess. Still pick one class_name, but set that entry's confidence to 0.3 so it is not
  auto-created against the guess, and list the other plausible (name, class_name) pairs in
  "candidates". Reserve a confidence above 0.5 for a class_name you are actually sure of.
- A student is "individually mentioned" ONLY if the teacher uses their name (or a
  recognizable nickname/variant of their name). Generic group references like "everyone",
  "all students", "the class" do NOT count as individual mentions.
- Do NOT create entries for students who are never individually mentioned by name. If a
  student is only covered by group-level observations (e.g. "the class was loud") but
  never called out by name, they must NOT appear in the output.
- Each student's quoted_text must contain ONLY (a) the observations the teacher made about
  that student and (b) group-level observations about that student's class. It MUST NOT
  contain an observation about any other named student, even one made in the same
  sentence. Never copy the whole transcript into every entry.
- A "group-level observation" is a statement about the class as a whole — it uses a
  collective referent such as "everyone", "all the kids", "the class", "they" (meaning the
  whole group). A statement that names a student, or describes only one student, is NEVER
  a group-level observation, no matter how it is joined to the rest of the sentence.
  Conjunctions and contrasts ("but", "and", "whereas", "while", "although", a comma) join
  separate individual observations; they do not merge them into one shared observation.
- Only group-level observations are shared between students. Append each one to the
  quoted_text of every individually-mentioned student in that class, wherever it fell in
  the transcript (beginning, middle, or end) and whoever was named next to it. Individual
  observations are never shared: they appear in exactly one entry, their own student's.
  Example A (a group observation is shared): Transcript says "Alice did great. Bob was
    quiet. The whole class struggled with fractions." → Alice's quoted_text is "Alice did
    great. The whole class struggled with fractions." and Bob's is "Bob was quiet. The
    whole class struggled with fractions." BOTH carry the fractions observation; NEITHER
    carries the other student's individual observation.
  Example B (one sentence, several students, nothing shared): Transcript says "Priya was
    on fire the whole hour, whereas Sam kept interrupting and Dan never opened his book."
    → Priya's quoted_text is "Priya was on fire the whole hour.", Sam's is "Sam kept
    interrupting.", Dan's is "Dan never opened his book." No collective referent appears,
    so nothing is shared and each entry names only its own student.
- If the transcript contains group references like "everyone", "all students", or "the
  class", apply those observations only to students in the class being discussed, not to
  ALL classes. Use context clues (class name mentions, prior student mentions) to
  determine which class is meant.
- Produce exactly one entry for every individually-mentioned student, in every class the
  transcript covers. A transcript that moves from one class to the next still owes an
  entry for each student named in each of them — do not stop after the first class.
- If a mentioned student cannot be matched to any roster entry, do not include them in the
  output
- If no students are clearly mentioned, return an empty students array
- The "class_name" field for each student MUST exactly match one of the class names from
  the roster above. Do not invent or abbreviate class names — if you are unsure which
  class a student belongs to, see the confidence/candidates rule above.
- IMPORTANT: Clean up speech into readable sentences, but do NOT invent observations or
  editorialize. Stay faithful to what the teacher actually said.
","role":"system"},{"content":"Um, so today I wanted to talk about Emma. She, uh, she did great in math today, really got the hang of the multiplication tables we've been working on. And then, let's see... I also wanted to mention Ryan. Ryan was, he was really struggling with the reading comprehension exercise, couldn't quite get the main idea from the passage. Yeah, that's, that's about it for today.","role":"user"}]
prompt.label: gradebee-prompt

Chloé is cooperative with peers and the teacher once focused, though she sometimes requires reminders to stay on task. Motivation and Participation

Chloé showed a positive attitude towards the activities. She was in a very good mood, and although she was a bit loud at the beginning, once the traffic light reminder was put in place she participated very well. She was open to new activities and showed interest in the new story tattoo and the what's missing activity. She also took an active part in the class work by repeating new vocabulary and structures and joining in with the story, worksheet, cleaning and dressing activities.

Behaviour

On this occasion, Chloé was quite distracted and tired, and she needed reminders to pay attention when workshop instructions were being given. When she was reminded, she settled down and stopped repeating her questions. The group was playful and loud at times, but could calm down with reminders, and Chloé remained involved in the group activities.

Learning

Chloé can repeat structures well and showed this with “Emma is wearing...”, the new vocabulary, and the new structures. She could tell her age and gender, almost always using the complete structure, and she could pair Emma’s dirty and clean body parts, although she sometimes needed the full structure to be reminded to her. Report Card for Camille · Class: Oliver · Group 2

Motivation and Participation

Camille demonstrates a positive attitude toward classroom activities, showing enthusiasm and engagement in most tasks. She enters the classroom with attentiveness and willingness to participate, particularly in activities she enjoys, such as "A Present for Me", the Dice Game, and Family Bingo. Her openness to new activities is evident, as she quickly adapts to routines like the weather and action miming, as well as the mood routine with phrases like "he's smiling because he's happy."

Camille is generally cooperative with peers and the teacher, though she occasionally engages in playful distractions with Zoé, such as jokingly hiding materials instead of returning them promptly when asked. Despite this, her interactions remain lighthearted, and she contributes to a positive group dynamic. Her participation is most pronounced in activities involving storytelling, vocabulary recall (e.g., colors, clothing, prepositions), and interactive games, where she shows strong memorization and understanding of the material. However, like her peers, she exhibits waning focus toward the end of longer activities, such as story recitation, where the group collectively grew bored.

While Camille is eager to engage in familiar or high-interest tasks, she occasionally holds back when less confident, as seen in her hesitation during new question-forming exercises (e.g., asking about physical appearance before guessing identities). Motivation and Participation

Motivation: Camille demonstrates a positive attitude toward classroom activities. She shows willingness to learn, as seen in her attentiveness during storytime and her enjoyment of new routines, such as the weather and action miming, as well as the mood routine. She is open to new activities, engaging enthusiastically with tasks like "A Present for Me," Family Bingo, and the Dice Game. Camille is generally cooperative with the group and the teacher, though she occasionally engages in playful behavior, such as hiding materials jokingly.

Participation: Camille actively participates in classroom activities, applying both previously acquired knowledge and new language. She recites parts of the story, remembers vocabulary well (including colors, clothing items, and prepositions), and quickly understands new routines. Her participation is strong when activities are engaging, such as "Who’s Missing" or the Dice Game. However, she sometimes holds back when less confident, as noted on a day when she was more hesitant, though encouragement helped her regain confidence.

Behaviour

Camille is generally well-integrated within the group, though she can be distracting at times, particularly when interacting playfully with peers like Zoé. She is attentive overall but may not always follow instructions immediately, such as returning materials when asked. Her behavior is influenced by the group’s mood—when the group is engaged, she participates actively, but she may also mirror their distractions. Camille’s mood appears to improve with encouragement, and she responds well to positive reinforcement.

Learning

  • Occasionally hesitant or less confident with new material; encouragement helps her overcome this.
  • Needs reminders for correct grammatical structures in some activities.
  • Sometimes playful or distracting with peers; will continue to reinforce classroom expectations.
  • Commitment: The school will continue to provide encouragement and structured reminders to build Camille’s confidence and consistency in applying language structures.

response.output:
Motivation and Participation

Camille showed a positive attitude towards the classroom activities. She was attentive overall and very attentive at times. She was very happy to listen to the story and seemed to really enjoy the new story. She loved the "Present for me" activity, as well as "Who's missing", Family Bingo, and the Dice Game. She also quickly understood the new weather and action miming routine, and the new mood routine with "he's smiling because he's happy".

She participated well in the activities and showed a real understanding of the worksheet work. She could do the worksheet activity about what Oliver and Baby could or couldn't do very well. She knew parts of the story and could recite the story partially. At the same time, she needed help to remember the correct structures for many activities, and she is still learning to ask questions about a person's physical appearance before asking who it is.

Behaviour

Camille was a bit distracting with Zoé, but it was alright. She was involved in Zoé being playful with the material, and at times she was not always giving the material back directly when asked, instead hiding it jokingly. By the end of the story, the group got bored. Camille was a bit less confident today and seemed more hesitant, but with encouragement she seemed quite happy.

Learning

Camille could remember the vocabulary words very well, and she could tell the colors and clothing items very well. She could also remember some prepositions. She showed a real understanding and a certain memorisation of the vocabulary, and she could repeat when asked. She quickly understood the new weather and action miming routine, as well as the new mood routine.

Her strengths are her vocabulary recall, her understanding of the worksheet activities, and her quick grasp of the new routines. Her areas for improvement are using the correct structures more independently, reciting the story more fully, and practising how to ask questions about physical appearance before identifying someone. We will continue to support her with these structures and with regular practice in class.
